newsitem.title: USA: Wall Street stocks seen opening flat to higher.
newsitem.headline: Wall Street stocks seen opening flat to higher.

text.p: Wall Street stocks are expected to open flat to slightly firmer Tuesday, but trading is likely to be defensive due to today's meeting of the policy-making Federal Open Market Committee.
U.S. housing starts in July, forecast at an annual rate of 1.46 million, a touch higher than in June, are due at 0830 EDT.

"The markets are going to be somewhat on the defensive usually until we hear from the FOMC, though nobody expects them to raise rates," said Peter Cardillo, director of research at Westfalia Investments.
The outcome of the FOMC meeting is expected at around 1415 EDT/1815 GMT.
The market will also be scrutinizing the tentative contract agreement between United Parcel Service and the Teamsters union ending a bitter 15-day strike.

Union President Ron Carey declared victory and said the Teamsters had won sweeping concessions for more full-time jobs, better pensions and improved pay that "sends a signal that American workers are on the move again."
Analysts took heart from Monday's late-afternoon rebound in the Dow, which closed up 108.7 points at 7803.36.
"This reinforces the theory that the investors are willing to buy on the dips," Cardillo said.
As in recent sessions, trading Monday was volatile.
U.S. Treasuries opened weaker today, with the long bond off 9/32 to yield 6.54 percent. The S&P 500 Futures September contract also traded lower, off 1.75 points at 917.00.
In Asia the dollar was confined to a narrow range against the yen in late Tokyo trade. The U.S. currency stood at 118.20/25 yen.
In Europe the dollar was underpinned by unchanged Bundesbank rates. It was trading at 1.8350/60 marks.
Japan's Nikkei 225 index closed down 80.10 points or 0.42 percent at 18,961.
In London the FTSE 100 was up 55.7 points or 1.15 percent at 4890.7.

The Wall Street Journal in its "Heard on the Street" column said the Grand Union supermarket chain may get an emergency loan of up to $75 million, and financier George Soros's investment firm may be among the lenders.

The New York Times's "Marketplace" column said the big three Swiss banks are staging a remarkable recovery from the worst year in their history, despite the black eye suffered for their handling of the accounts of victims of the Nazis.
